newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German media summit to break digital logjam.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German media summit to break digital logjam.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom chairman Ron Sommer, Bertelsmann chief Mark Woessner and Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch will meet top executives and state politicians for a German media summit next month, industry sources said on Monday.

The high-level conference is a last-ditch bid to break a deadlock over the expansion of German cable television networks and the introduction of broadscale digital TV programming, which industry squabbling has held up for nearly two years.

Chaired by Deutsche Telekom, the meeting will take place on May 20 and include the heads of Germany's three largest commercial TV stations, all-news channel N-TV, public network ARD and rival cable TV operators such as Veba AG, a shareholder in the O.Tel.O communications group.

State media regulators, economics ministers and the heads of state cabinet offices, who under German law are responsible for regulating the media, will also attend, which sources said could help speed a solution of the politically-charged dispute.

"The issues are developing a common strategy for the future development of the television industry and the expansion of the cable TV networks in both analogue and digital," said one industry source who asked not to be identified.
Deutsche Telekom declined to comment on the meeting.

Last month it invited representatives of media, government and other telecoms companies to "round table" talks to resolve a frustrating industry dispute over digital television and reorganisation of cable TV networks.

Telekom wants to finally clarify the technical standards for digital TV decoders, questions regarding expansion of its cable TV network, regulatory issues involving so-called "must carry" programming, and a new cable TV billing model.

In the past broadcasters paid Telekom a nominal fee to be carried by the cable network and state media regulators decided which channels would fill the tight analogue network, limited to around 30 channels.
But with the advent of telecoms deregulation and 150 digital channels ready to go, Telekom wants to change the rules of the game.
It now wants to pay broadcasters, much the way its counterparts in the United States and Britain buy programming.
And it wants to decide itself which programming appears on its cable network and create packages with different price ranges from basic to premium.
In exchange, it would guarantee a certain number of basic channels, probably the main commercial and public channels, as "must carry" programmes to be chosen by media regulators.

Telekom's Sommer has said programming that appeals to small audiences -- like foreign-language channels like CNN or NBC Super Channel -- should be put in special packages that required an additional fee.
Much to the displeasure of Kirch and pay TV channel Premiere, Telekom wants to manage subscriptions to the new line-up of pay TV and other cable offerings it is planning.

It wants these issues to be cleared up before an International Broadcasting Exhibition in Berlin in August so that new cable TV packages including digital TV programming can be offered to the public in time for Christmas.

But it must first settle a dispute with Kirch over the basic decoder technology for digital television which has kept Kirch's DF1 channel out of cable TV networks. It must also strike a deal with Premiere, which has over 1.5 million subscribers, and a compromise to share revenue with rival cable firms.
Sommer told Der Spiegel magazine this week that he was close to a deal with Kirch.

"When this consensus has been reached, it is unimportant what a decoder looks like technically or who sells it," he said. "It does not matter which video recorder you use as long as it operates according to the VHS standard."
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097150
